I've been farming this same land in Quzhou for over fifty years. My husband is gone, my son works in Shijiazhuang, and I manage about 4 mu on my own. I'm 75, my knees ache in the cold, so I pay the village tractor service to do the heavy work — plowing, seeding, harvesting. That's just how things are now.

I'll do what I've always done: wheat in the ground after the autumn equinox, corn after the wheat comes off in June. The two fit together perfectly, one plot, two crops, one year. I've never tried vegetables or anything else — I don't have the energy for that kind of daily tending, and I don't know those markets.

For wheat, I'll buy the improved seeds from the village supply co-op, same variety as last year — the agent said it did well on heavy clay soil like mine. I apply compound fertilizer when I plant, then spread urea by hand when it starts to green up in spring. I'll call for irrigation three times: once before winter sets in hard, once at jointing, once when the grain is filling. I put on herbicide in early spring and spray once more for aphids if I see them.

For maize, I use hybrid seed — I've used hybrid corn for thirty years, the yields are much better. I scatter fertilizer when the seedlings are knee-high. Summer rain usually handles most of the water, but I'll irrigate once if July is dry. One pesticide spray is usually enough unless the corn borer is bad.

I don't plow for maize — I just plant directly into the wheat stubble after the combine goes through. Saves money, saves my back.
